brief.topic: A Larger Pattern Hidden Between Two Sheets

s01: These broad bands are not drawn on either sheet.
Each sheet contains only evenly spaced lines.
A small rotation lets the larger pattern appear.
This is a moire pattern.
Where the lines overlap, more of the pale background remains.
Between those places, the dark lines cover more of the page.
Our eyes can follow that slower change.
The two fine patterns create a much wider rhythm.
Let us pause the rotation and look at the geometry.
Both sheets have the same small spacing, called p.
Their directions differ by ten degrees.
As we move across the sheets, their mismatch accumulates.
After one whole line spacing of relative shift,
the alignment repeats.
The distance between alignment bands is much larger than p.
For these equal grids, geometry gives this relationship.
Divide p by twice the sine of half the angle.
At ten degrees, the bands are about five point seven times wider.
Turn to twenty degrees and they become about two point nine times wider.
A smaller angle makes the large pattern spread out.
At exactly zero angle, the repeating bands disappear.
The matching sheets simply lie on top of each other.
This visible pattern comes from overlap.
We do not need wave interference to explain it.
A slight difference can become a large, visible structure.
